findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27, 02/09/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: The council faces a £6.8m forecast budget gap in 2028/29, with core spending power increases well below the national average.
findings.detail: St Helens is forecast to receive only 1.3% core spending power increase in 2027/28 and 1.5% in 2028/29, compared to national average increases of 4.3% and 4.4% respectively. Directorates have been tasked with finding 1.5% efficiencies per annum. The quantum of funding reduces in the final two years of the three-year settlement.
findings.matters: The council is receiving below-average funding while demand pressures mount; the 2028/29 gap will require further significant savings when the council is already struggling to deliver current-year savings.
findings.figures: £6.8m forecast budget gap in 2028/29; core spending power growth 2027/28 1.3% (national average 4.3%); 2028/29 1.5% (national average 4.4%)
findings.quote: There is a forecast budget gap in the final year of the settlement period 2028/29 of £6.8m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27, 02/09/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: The council requires approximately £90m of borrowing to fund its capital programme and regeneration schemes.
findings.detail: Historically, the council used internal resources to fund capital investment and is under-borrowed. However, as internal resources deplete, borrowing is necessary. In July 2026, the council borrowed £5m from another local authority at 4.65% for one year. Borrowing rates remain elevated due to geopolitical volatility. Movements in rates will not impact the current fixed-rate portfolio but will increase the cost of future borrowing.
findings.matters: The council will incur significant additional debt servicing costs as internal resources deplete; combined with revenue overspend, this will squeeze the budget further and require either substantial savings or service reductions.
findings.figures: Approximately £90m borrowing requirement for capital programme; £5m borrowed in July 2026 at 4.65% for one year; current borrowing £162.478m as at 31 July 2026
findings.quote: When setting the budget, the need to borrow a significant amount of circa £90m to fund the Council's capital programme and committed regeneration schemes in the current year was assumed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27, 02/09/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: The Dedicated Schools Grant is forecasting a £12.793m in-year pressure, driven by insufficient High Needs Block funding for EHCP demand.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit is held in a separate reserve and does not impact the general fund under a statutory override valid to 31 March 2028. The pressure reflects continued growth in Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs). The council is pursuing SEND reform and may become eligible for High Needs Stability Funding, but final approval and financial implications are not yet confirmed.
findings.matters: The DSG statutory override expires in 2028; accumulated deficits will then impact the general fund, representing a deferred liability that will worsen the council's position in future years unless resolved.
findings.figures: £12.793m in-year DSG pressure; held in separate reserve under statutory override to 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The underlying financial challenge remains that available funding within the High Needs Block is insufficient to meet current levels of demand, particularly given the continued growth in the number of pupils with Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27, 02/09/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Home to School Transport is forecasting a £1.500m overspend driven by demand from children with SEND requiring specialist provision.
findings.detail: This pressure is driven by 'increasing demand associated with children and young people with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), particularly those requiring transport to specialist provision'. The service is exploring mitigation options including independent travel training, personalised travel budgets, and route optimisation, with a new policy to be consulted in Autumn, but cost controls are not keeping pace with demand growth.
findings.matters: SEND-related transport demand is a national trend growing faster than funding; this signals a structural pressure that will persist and likely worsen unless the national SEND funding model changes.
findings.figures: £1.500m overspend in Home to School Transport (part of £7.617m Children & Young People overspend)
findings.quote: Home to School Transport is forecasting an overspend of £1.500m. The pressure continues to be driven by increasing demand associated with children and young people with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), particularly those requiring transport to specialist provision.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27, 02/09/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: General Fund balance is forecast to fall to £8.983m by 31 March 2027, below the approved prudent level of £14.6m.
findings.detail: The council approved a Reserves Strategy targeting £14.6m in general fund balances to cushion against uncertainty. The current forecast position of £8.983m represents a £5.617m reduction due to the net overspend. The report warns that if the trend of previous years continues, the use of earmarked reserves will again be necessary to replenish general fund balances, undermining the Reserves Strategy.
findings.matters: General fund depletion limits the council's ability to respond to unexpected events or service pressures and signals reliance on one-off earmarked reserves rather than sustainable budgeting.
findings.figures: General Fund balance at 31 March 2026: £12.0m; target by 31 March 2027: £14.6m; actual forecast: £8.983m; required minimum: £14.6m
findings.quote: If the financial position can be brought back to a balanced position or better, this will be the first year since 2021/22 that the transfer of earmarked reserves to maintain the general fund at a prudent level will not be required.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27, 02/09/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Only 70.87% of approved savings are forecast to be delivered, leaving £1.625m at risk of non-delivery.
findings.detail: Of the £5.579m total savings requirement, only £3.954m (70.87%) are forecast to be delivered on track. £1.625m (29.13%) may not be fully delivered due to implementation delays. Temporary mitigations of £0.401m have been identified, but permanent alternatives must be found for the remainder. The report flags this as creating 'a severe risk for both current and future financial years'.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver approved savings in full means the £5.617m overspend will not improve without additional measures, and undelivered recurring savings will create structural deficits in future years.
findings.figures: £5.579m total savings requirement; £3.954m on track (70.87%); £1.625m at risk (29.13%); £0.401m temporary mitigation identified
findings.quote: The non-achievement of permanent savings presents a severe risk for both current and future financial years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27, 02/09/2026 Cabinet
findings.headline: Children looked after placements are forecasting a combined £7.451m overspend, driven by external residential and fostering provision.
findings.detail: The Children & Young People portfolio is reporting a £7.617m total overspend, with £7.451m relating to children looked after placements, particularly external residential and fostering provision. The service is attempting to reduce reliance through in-house provision and local placement options, but transitions are still being progressed and have not yet delivered cost reductions.
findings.matters: External placements represent the council's highest-cost statutory service provision; unchecked growth signals escalating child protection demand and loss of financial control over a critical function.
findings.figures: £7.451m combined overspend on children looked after placements; £7.617m total Children & Young People portfolio overspend
findings.quote: The most significant financial pressures continue to relate to the cost of placements for children looked after, particularly the use of external residential and fostering provision, which is forecasting a combined overspend of £7.451m.

findings.matters: Persistent overspending across five consecutive years indicates structural budget pressures that cannot be managed through one-off measures, raising fundamental questions about the sustainability of the council's financial position.

findings.quote: Unless the Council can bring these costs under control by the end of the year, 2026/27 will be the 5th successive year the Council has overspent against its approved budget.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27
findings.headline: Adult Social Care placement costs rising 16-21% over two years; dependency on price stabilisation continuing
findings.detail: The council reports that 'the average price of a supported living placement has risen by 21% in the last two years. Similarly, the average price of a package of residential and nursing care has risen by 17% and 16% respectively, over the same time period.' While the report notes 'most of that increase was incurred in the 2024-2025 financial year, with price rises flattening off during since mid-2025,' the Adult Social Care portfolio is forecast to balance only 'based on the assumption that sufficient measures will be put in place to manage the increasing demand.' The portfolio faces £4.4m in unaddressed demand pressures.
findings.matters: Care placement cost inflation at this scale (16-21% over 2 years) far exceeds general inflation and cannot be sustained indefinitely. The council is managing this year by assuming it can hold price growth flat, but this is fragile and dependent on market conditions. Further price inflation would force either additional budget pressure or service reduction.
findings.figures: Supported living up 21% in 2 years; residential/nursing care up 17% and 16%; £4.4m unaddressed demand pressure; nursing care numbers +6% since February 2026; CHC funding down 19%

Combined with current-year overspending and a structural SEND funding problem, the 2028/29 position represents a medium-term affordability challenge that will require either major service cuts or additional reserves use.

This defers major capital investment decisions.
findings.matters: Deferring £90m of planned capital borrowing signals financial stress. While rate management is normal, deferring capital investment due to both cost and financial position suggests the council may not be able to afford the borrowing even at better rates. This is a concern for service delivery and sustainability.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27
findings.headline: General Fund balances forecast to fall £5.617m to £8.983m, below prudent level of £14.6m
findings.detail: The council's General Fund balance is forecast to drop from a planned £14.6m target to £8.983m by 31 March 2027 — a shortfall of £5.617m. The report states that 'if the financial position can be brought back to a balanced position or better, this will be the first year since 2021/22 that the transfer of earmarked reserves to maintain the general fund at a prudent level (£14.6m from 2026/27) will not be required.' It then warns: 'if the trend of previous years continues the use of earmarked reserves will again be necessary in 2026/27 to replenish general fund balances.'
findings.matters: Reserves are a council's shock absorber. Repeated drawdowns to cover revenue overspends (rather than one-off items) signal that revenue spending is unsustainable. Five years of this pattern is unsustainable. A lender reviews reserves as liquidity and affordability cover.
findings.figures: £14.6m prudent target; £8.983m forecast 31 March 2027; £5.617m drawdown; 5 successive years of earmarked reserve drawdown required
findings.quote: if the financial position can be brought back to a balanced position or better, this will be the first year since 2021/22 that the transfer of earmarked reserves to maintain the general fund at a prudent level (£14.6m from 2026/27) will not be required. This position aligns to the approved Reserves Strategy, which identifies the Council's required level of general balances as being £14.6m. It should be noted that the position at the end of Quarter 1 is already projecting a significant overspend and if the trend of previous years continues the use of earmarked reserves will again be necessary in 2026/27 to replenish general fund balances.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27

findings.detail: Of £5.579m in approved budget savings, only £3.954m (70.87%) is forecast to be delivered in-year. £1.625m (29.13%) is at risk due to implementation delays. Only £0.401m of temporary mitigations have been identified for the slipped amount, leaving a gap of £1.224m. The report notes 'it is critical that action plans continue to be addressed and implemented to ensure that savings are delivered or alternative permanent reductions in expenditure are found.'
findings.matters: Savings shortfalls are a leading indicator of future budget stress. When a council can deliver only 71% of planned savings at Q1, it signals either weak planning, execution risk, or unachievable savings targets. This feeds into the overspend problem.
findings.figures: £5.579m total savings required; £3.954m (70.87%) on track; £1.625m (29.13%) at risk; £0.401m temporary mitigations; £1.224m unmitigated gap
findings.quote: Of the £1.625m of savings that have not yet been achieved, temporary mitigations of £0.401m have been identified / are in the process of being developed. Further work is needed to ensure these savings are delivered in full on a recurring basis to negate pressures on the current year and future years budget.

findings.paper_title: Item 5 - Appendix 1 - Financial Monitoring Report Period 1 2026-27

findings.matters: This is a growing national problem affecting many councils, but the scale here (£12.8m) and the council's dependence on a government reform funding decision that hasn't been confirmed represents a material contingent liability and structural sustainability risk. The statutory override ends in 2028.
findings.figures: £12.793m in-year DSG pressure; statutory override until 31 March 2028; growing EHCP numbers
findings.quote: High Needs funding primarily supports provision for children and young people with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) who require additional support to access education. findings.headline: Adult Social Care & Health £1.5m overspend from ongoing demand and rising care package costs
findings.detail: Adult social care shows forecast overspend of £1.5m, worsening from £1.2m at Period 2. The driver is ongoing demand pressures and increases in the cost of individual care packages.
findings.matters: Demand-driven pressures in an ageing population represent a structural budget challenge that cannot be easily reduced and may continue to deteriorate.
findings.figures: £1.5m overspend at P3 (£1.2m at P2)
findings.quote: The other main pressure is within Adult Social Care & Health, reflecting ongoing demand pressures and the increases in the cost of individual care packages.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring Report Period 3 202526 Cover
findings.headline: Children & Young People services overspend doubled to £7.747m, driven by staffing and placement cost pressures
findings.detail: The Children & Young People portfolio shows the largest single overspend, more than double the Period 2 position. Drivers are social work staffing challenges, unachieved savings, and placement costs. Agency staff reduction plans are in place but implementation is slow, and Ofsted registration delays have hampered savings delivery.
findings.matters: Once social care placements are made, they are sticky costs difficult to reverse; doubling of this pressure in six months signals accelerating demand and cost control issues.
findings.figures: £7.747m overspend at P3 (£3.817m at P2); represents largest single portfolio pressure
findings.quote: The main pressure is within Children & Young People, the main drivers of this being social work staffing challenges, unachieved savings and placement costs. A plan is in place to reduce the reliance upon agency staff but this will take time to implement, and the delivery of savings has been hampered in this financial year due to delays in Ofsted registration.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring Report Period 3 202526 Cover
findings.headline: Fourth consecutive year of budget overspend, worsening from £3.119m to £5.448m
findings.detail: The council's forecast overspend has deteriorated at Period 3 compared to Period 2. External auditors Grant Thornton have flagged the council's financial position and made specific recommendations on financial management, indicating auditor concern about the trajectory.
findings.matters: A pattern of four consecutive years of overspend combined with audit concern signals persistent financial control issues and depleting reserves sustainability.
findings.figures: £5.448m net forecast overspend 2025/26; £3.119m at Period 2; portfolio overspend £9.117m against net budget of £203.172m
findings.quote: The forecast position has worsened compared to the overspend position within the 2025/26 FMR 2 and will result in a fourth consecutive year of overspend. Breaking the cycle of overspends is a key milestone for the Council's financial stability over the medium term.

findings.paper_title: C - MTFS 2026-2029 and Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Council must begin to establish better control over demand-led spending in children's and adult social care
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer identifies a need to 'manage the demand and price pressures, specifically within children's services and adult social care, such that the Council can begin to better control its expenditure'. The phrasing 'begin to better control' indicates expenditure in these areas has not been well-controlled historically.
findings.matters: This is a critical condition for medium-term budget stability. If demand-led services continue to exceed budget, reserves will deplete rapidly and Section 114 risk will escalate.
findings.figures: Not quantified as separate budget line
findings.quote: To manage the demand and price pressures, specifically within children's services and adult social care, such that the Council can begin to better control its expenditure

findings.paper_title: C - MTFS 2026-2029 and Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Borrowing capacity is explicitly constrained by revenue budget pressures; capital investment will be limited by affordability
findings.detail: The council states that 'the revenue budget position remains challenging' and that any capital borrowing 'will need to be carefully considered and the revenue impact remain affordable'. The capital programme exceeds £224m over three years but cannot assume unconstrained borrowing to fund it.
findings.matters: For lenders assessing debt capacity and covenant headroom, this signals the council's ability to borrow is limited. Capital priorities may be deferred or scaled, affecting long-term asset management.
findings.figures: Capital programme estimated value exceeds £224 million over 2026-2029
findings.quote: As the revenue budget position remains challenging, any increases to borrowing to fund schemes will need to be carefully considered and the revenue impact remain affordable.

findings.paper_title: C - MTFS 2026-2029 and Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: The council is dependent on the full 4.99% Council Tax increase; reducing it would increase likelihood of future service cuts
findings.detail: The council explicitly recommends the full 4.99% Council Tax increase (2% ASC precept plus 2.99% general increase). The paper warns that any reduction below this limit would have 'material consequences and increase the likelihood of future reductions in services', signalling this income is essential to budget balance and the council has no contingency if tax growth is restricted.
findings.matters: Revenue dependency on tax maximisation reduces resilience. Any variance in collection, policy constraint, or electorate resistance would immediately force further savings or reserve depletion.
findings.figures: Band D Council Tax £1,975.65; total Council Tax Requirement £106.727 million
findings.quote: Any proposal to reduce the Council Tax uplift below the 4.99% referendum limit would have material consequences and increase the likelihood of future reductions in services.

findings.paper_title: C - MTFS 2026-2029 and Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Adult social care cost pressures are significant and public opposition to proposed savings is documented
findings.detail: The paper acknowledges 'significant budget pressure areas within services' with 'market pressures' particularly in social care, addressed through budget uplifts. However, consultation responses show the majority of residents found proposed savings in domiciliary care hours, mental health floating support, and adult respite services 'disagreeable'. The equality impact assessment identifies these will have 'potential cumulative negative impact on disabled and older people'.
findings.matters: Implementation risk: if savings cannot be delivered due to service quality issues, public pressure, or increased need, unplanned spending will destabilise the budget quickly. Demand-led services are difficult to control once political resistance emerges.
findings.figures: Not quantified in headline budget figures
findings.quote: Adult and Older People Social Care savings options linked to domiciliary care hours, Internal and external mental health floating support service, and the review of respite services for adults with a learning disability, were all felt to be disagreeable by the majority of respondents.

findings.paper_title: C - MTFS 2026-2029 and Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: The entire budget balance is conditional on full delivery of previously approved savings; no alternative is identified
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that savings are 'imperative' to deliver a balanced budget. The budget contains no growth and assumes all approved savings will be delivered in full during 2026/27 and the medium term. Failure to deliver any savings creates a gap with no identified alternative funding or service reduction mechanism.
findings.matters: If savings do not materialise as planned, the council will draw on reserves or seek Exceptional Financial Support. Budget dependency on prior approvals is a delivery and political risk that lenders must assess.
findings.figures: Council Tax Requirement £106.727 million (balanced on savings delivery)
findings.quote: It is imperative that the savings options agreed are progressed and delivered in 2026/27 and over the medium term in order to provide a budget that is balanced based on the current assumptions and projections.

findings.paper_title: C - MTFS 2026-2029 and Revenue & Capital Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Section 114 Notice risk is acknowledged as substantial and likely in the future if budget conditions fail
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer explicitly states that whilst the risk of issuing a Section 114 Notice is not imminent during this MTFS period, it is substantial and likely in the future. The risk materialises if any of three critical conditions fail: delivering approved savings, managing demand pressures in children's and adult social care, or identifying new efficiencies by 2028/29. Reserve depletion or Exceptional Financial Support would likely precede this.
findings.matters: A Section 114 Notice (statutory spending prohibition) is the most serious financial distress indicator. For lenders, it signals potential inability to service debt or meet statutory obligations.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: Whilst the risk of the Council having to issue a Section 114 Notice is substantial i.e. it is likely in the future, it is not yet likely over the period of this Medium Term Financial Strategy.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Scrutiny Task Group - Final Report
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review increases revenue nominally but does not increase actual spending power; Council Tax rise is still required to balance
findings.detail: The Commission notes that while government funding increased through the Fair Funding Review and changes to deprivation formulas, these gains are entirely consumed by cost increases the council faces. Previous ringfenced grants have been merged into general funding, creating a visual increase that masks no real fiscal gain. The council still requires a Council Tax rise to balance the budget.
findings.matters: Structural funding squeeze with no headroom for growth or investment; dependent on Council Tax increases to maintain service levels, which is politically and operationally constrained.
findings.figures: No specific percentages; described as merger of "previously ringfenced budgets into the base Grant."
findings.quote: The Commission understands the merging of previously ringfenced budgets into the base Grant give the appearance that the Council is receiving more funding but this is simply a repackaging of grants and there will still be a requirement to increase Council Tax rates to generate a balanced budget

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Scrutiny Task Group - Final Report
findings.headline: 2026/27 is the final year of the current MTFS with minimal fiscal flexibility
findings.detail: The budget scrutiny focused on how the council would stick to the existing MTFS rather than proposing new initiatives, with explicit recognition that there is "little room within budgets for additional spending or savings" in this final year.
findings.matters: End of planning cycle creates uncertainty about the next MTFS; constrained flexibility now may lead to sharp adjustments when the new plan is set.
findings.figures: MTFS set by Council in March 2024; 2026/27 is year three of three.
findings.quote: with 2026/27 being the third and final year of the current MTFS there was little room within budgets for additional spending or savings, and every penny needed to be managed effectively

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Budget Scrutiny Task Group - Final Report
findings.headline: Council is experiencing overspends this year from demand in Children's and Adults' Social Care and SEN education
findings.detail: The Commission notes overspends have occurred in the current year and recognises persistent budget pressures from high demand in statutory social care services. These pressures arise from both increased demand and inflated external provision costs, which are difficult to mitigate given statutory duties.
findings.matters: Current-year overspends signal operational financial control weakness and whether demand growth is outpacing budget allocation.
findings.figures: No specific numbers given; report notes this is a year-on-year pattern.
findings.quote: The Commission notes the overspends that have occurred this year and recognises the persistent reasons for budget pressures from high levels of demand in Adults and Children's Social Care and SEN education provision
